rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **"Indivisible" vs "indestructible":** indivisible = cannot be split (false — subatomic particles); indestructible = cannot be created/destroyed in chemical reactions (true for chemistry).  ·  **Isotope vs allotrope:** isotopes are atoms of the same element with different mass (¹²C, ¹⁴C); allotropes are different structural forms of the same element (diamond, graphite).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Matter is composed of extremely small, indivisible particles called atoms" — Dalton, 1803.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***CO vs CO₂*** — carbon and oxygen combine 12:16 and 12:32; the oxygen masses per fixed carbon are in the ratio 1:2 — Dalton's own multiple-proportions example.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The First Quantitative Model of Matter John Dalton (1803–1808, *A New System of Chemical Philosophy*) proposed the first quantitative atomic theory to explain the newly discovered laws of chemical combination. It turned chemistry from a qualitative craft into a quantitative science — every stoichiometric calculation you will ever do rests on his postulates.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The postulates (state them in order — NEB 2–3m) 1. **Indivisibility:** matter consists of extremely small, indivisible particles called **atoms**. 2. **Identity:** atoms of the same element are identical in mass, size and chemical properties; atoms of different elements differ in all these. 3.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Limitations = DIVisible, ISotopes, COMplex ratios — remember DIC."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): State three limitations of Dalton's atomic theory with one example each.** — (1) Atoms are divisible: electron (1897), proton, neutron are subatomic particles. (2) Atoms of the same element are not identical: isotopes ¹H and ²H differ in mass.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: When asked for limitations, give at least three with one example each (electron, isotope ¹H/²H, Fe₀.₉₅O).

rows.label: Classified table
rows.text: 2.2 Successes — what the theory explained · Law explained | Dalton's reasoning · Conservation of mass (Lavoisier) | Atoms are only rearranged, never lost · Definite proportions (Proust) | Fixed atom ratios give fixed mass ratios · Multiple proportions (Dalton) | Two elements can combine in more than one whole-number ratio (CO, CO₂) · Basis of stoichiometry | Balancing equations = conserving atoms of each element  ·  2.3 Limitations (exam-critical — NEB asks this repeatedly) · Limitation | Why it fails · Atoms ARE divisible | Electron (1897), proton, neutron — subatomic particles exist · Atoms of an element are identical | **Isotopes** (¹H, ²H, ³H; ³⁵Cl, ³⁷Cl) differ in mass · Atoms combine in simple ratios | Non-stoichiometric compounds (Fe₀.₉₅O) and complex ratios exist · Atom is the smallest reacting unit | Molecules react as units; ions and electrons react too ·…

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Isotopes break postulate 2** — atoms of the same element are NOT all identical in mass; this is the classic limitation NEB asks.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Dalton (1803–1808): atoms indivisible, identical per element, indestructible in reactions, combine in whole-number ratios. Explains conservation of mass, definite and multiple proportions. Limitations: subatomic particles, isotopes, non-stoichiometry.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Dalton's theory is the birth of modern chemistry: it made mass the currency of chemical reasoning.

rows.label: MCQ drill
